title: Eight parts of a path
hook: the fourth truth: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration

segments.voice: Yesterday: nibbana, a flame going out. Your line was a flame that has gone out. Did you catch one wanting that went out on its own? Today, the last of the four truths, and the end of the week. Day seven hundred seven.

Three truths in, a practical question shows up. Fine. Suffering has a plain name. The thirst behind it has been found. And it can end, like a lamp going out. So what happens on Wednesday morning, with the dishes and the commute and the email that needs answering? The Buddha's first teaching doesn't leave that hanging. Its fourth truth isn't another idea. It's a path. And the path comes in eight parts, most of which look a lot like an ordinary day.
screen: `THREE TRUTHS IN.` → `SO WHAT HAPPENS ON WEDNESDAY?` → `THE FOURTH TRUTH IS A PATH.`

segments.voice: First, a middle way. In the Samyutta Nikaya, before he names any of the four truths, the Buddha names two roads to avoid. One is chasing sense pleasures. The other is tormenting yourself. Both, he says, are unprofitable. Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is this path. Second, the eight parts. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration. Say them slowly and notice how few of them happen on a cushion. Speech is what comes out at the checkout. Action is what the hands do. Livelihood is how the rent gets paid. Third, a nun sorts them. In the Majjhima Nikaya, a layman puts questions to the nun Dhammadinna, and she answers him. One answer groups the eight into three. Speech, action and livelihood belong to virtue. Effort, mindfulness and concentration belong to concentration. View and intention belong to wisdom. So the path has a shape: how you live with others, how you train the mind, and how you see. Fourth, one step at a time. Look back at the week. The second arrow and the thirst. Hatred that ends only by love, and the mind that leads. Patacara's grief and her lamp, and nibbana. All of that circled the first three truths: what hurts, where it comes from, and that it can end. The fourth truth is the one you walk. And nobody walks eight steps at once. A path of eight parts is still walked one step at a time, on one ordinary day, starting with whichever step the day hands you.
screen: `A MIDDLE WAY BETWEEN TWO ROADS.` · `EIGHT PARTS, MOSTLY ORDINARY.` · `DHAMMADINNA SORTS THEM INTO THREE.` · `ONE STEP AT A TIME.` · then, large: `ONE STEP OF EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Now walk through the eight, slowly, one per breath. View. Intention. Speech. Action. Livelihood. Effort. Mindfulness. Concentration. On the second time through, notice which one catches. Maybe speech, because of a conversation coming later. Maybe effort, because something has been put off. Let that one stay, and let the others rest. Then see where today will meet it: the room, the person, the hour. Just see it. The bell holds the time.
Middle way, the Buddha's fourth noble truth: a path of eight parts, between chasing pleasure and tormenting yourself, walked one step at a time. Today's word.
Your line: one step of eight. Keep the one part you picked with you today, and when its moment comes, the conversation or the chore, take that one step on purpose. Day seven hundred seven.

howItsDone: Buddhists study the noble eightfold path as the fourth noble truth; in daily life practitioners often work with one factor at a time, such as right speech or right livelihood, alongside meditation for effort, mindfulness and concentration.

match.prompt: inside the fourth truth — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: you're one of the Buddha's first listeners. he names two roads to avoid: chasing sense pleasure, and tormenting yourself. what does he offer?
options: a little of each, in balance
the harder road, since pleasure is the trap
a middle way: a path with eight parts
fork.reveal: he calls both roads unprofitable and names a middle way between them: the noble eightfold path, the fourth truth.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: the path with eight parts, from the Buddha's first teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: the eightfold path is a list of rules to obey.
what it means: the fourth truth: eight parts of one middle way, from view and intention through speech, action and livelihood to effort, mindfulness and concentration.
what a scholar hears: the path of the first teaching (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11), and Dhammadinna's grouping of it into virtue, concentration and wisdom in Majjhima Nikaya 44.
recall: live as one who wants to be him

notes: Editor: week look-back reworded; it had said the week 'walked the truths in order', though hatred and the mind that leads are Dhammapada days, not truths.

SN 56.11 paraphrased: the two extremes (devotion to sense pleasures, devotion to self-mortification), both called unprofitable; the middle way identified as the noble eightfold path, whose eight factors are listed. Confirm the gloss 'unprofitable'.

MN 44 paraphrased: the layman Visakha questions the nun Dhammadinna; she says the three aggregates (virtue, concentration, wisdom) are included in the eightfold path, with speech/action/livelihood under virtue, effort/mindfulness/concentration under concentration, view/intention under wisdom. Confirm.

Original: aṭṭhaṅgika magga in Devanagari and the stress in 'say' should be checked by a Pali reader.
The phrase 'nobody walks eight steps at once' is the script's own image, not a claim about how the factors are developed; Buddhist schools describe the relation among the factors in different ways.
